I Tried CloudWatch Omni a Day After Launch: Instrumenting and Evaluating a Strands Agent Locally in Kiro

CloudWatch Omni launched on September 22. I wanted to answer one question: does it tell me anything about an AI agent that CloudWatch metrics wouldn't?

Key Highlights

  • Onboarding is agent-driven: the extension hands setup to Kiro through an MCP server and skill files you can read in your repo.
  • Windows is its own path: programmatic initialize() loading, and a bash-style .env.omni that PowerShell can't source.
  • Traces caught a bug the output hid: a mangled "Where input showed up as 7 LLM traces but only 3 tool calls.
  • 31 evaluators out of the box, and a Playground where Helpfulness caught what two other evaluators missed.
  • Prompt versions link to traces: after moving the prompt into prompts.json, Omni listed the trace produced by v1.

This is Part 1. I stayed in the local dev loop: the Omni IDE extension inside Kiro, a small Strands agent, Nova 2 Lite on Bedrock, and a Windows laptop. No cloud space, no online evaluations, no alarms. That's Part 2.

Section 01

What is CloudWatch Omni?

CloudWatch Omni is a new AI-powered observability experience built on top of CloudWatch, for applications and AI agents together. It reads the same logs, metrics, and traces you already send to CloudWatch, so nothing you run today changes. You use it outside the AWS console, through a web app with SSO or an extension in VS Code, Kiro, or Cursor. On top of the usual signals, it adds auto-discovered service maps, plain-English queries, AI-assisted investigations, and quality scoring for agent answers.

A few examples of what that means in practice:

  • A food-delivery support agent (think Swiggy or Zomato) answers politely but wrong. Error rate stays at 0% because nothing crashed. An Omni evaluator scores the answer as incorrect or off-topic, and you see it next to the latency and tokens on the same trace.
  • A checkout API slows down during a sale. Omni's application map shows which downstream service is dragging, and an alert can open an investigation with AWS DevOps Agent to find the cause.
  • Someone edits the agent's system prompt on Friday. With prompt versions linked to traces, you can see that scores dropped for traces from v2 but not v1, and roll back.
  • You ask "why did latency spike on the payments service?" instead of writing a query. Omni writes the SQL or PromQL for you.

This post covers the agent side, locally. Part 2 covers the cloud side.

Section 02

The agent

A food-delivery support agent with two tools, get_order_status and start_refund. The system prompt says it only handles orders, refunds, and delivery issues. It's a CLI: you pass a question, it prints an answer. requirements.txt has two lines: aws-opentelemetry-distro>=0.20.0 and strands-agents.

Section 03

Step 0: Finding the extension

Tip

Searching "omni" in the extensions panel is a mess. Quota managers, file browsers, formatters, and a media viewer all show up before AWS. The one you want is Amazon CloudWatch Omni by amazonwebservices. Search "CloudWatch Omni" and save yourself the scroll.

Searching "omni" returns a lot of unrelated extensions

When I installed it, it was version 1.0.0, published 7 hours earlier, with 146 installs. The listing describes it as agent observability, testing, and evals in the editor: debug OpenTelemetry traces, replay runs in a playground, and measure changes, locally or in your AWS account.

The extension listing, version 1.0.0

After install, a Welcome to Omni tab opens with two options: let a coding assistant set everything up, or configure manually.

Welcome screen with Quick configuration

Section 04

Step 1: Pick a coding assistant, let it onboard you

The Quick configuration screen asks which coding assistant should do the setup. The list showed Kiro, Claude Code, and Codex as IDE options, plus Claude Code CLI and Kiro CLI under terminal, each marked installed or not.

Choosing a coding assistant

I picked Kiro. The extension said it had configured Kiro with its tools and skills, and gave me an Onboard with Kiro button.

Kiro configured with Omni tools and skills

That button opens a Kiro session with a pre-written prompt. It tells Kiro to use the onboarding skill, points it at one MCP server called cw-omni-agents-extension, and asks it to report every step back to the extension's UI through a notify_ui tool.

The generated onboarding prompt

One small wobble: Kiro first looked for the Omni tools as a Kiro "power," didn't find them, then worked out the MCP server was configured directly. It recovered on its own, but it's the kind of thing that confuses you if you're watching closely.

Kiro working out where the Omni tools live

Every MCP call asks for approval: Allow, Always allow, Deny. Slow if you click through each one, but you see exactly what's being called.

Approval prompt for notify_ui

Section 05

What it drops into your project

Two folders appear.

.omni/ holds local state: collector.json, evaluators.json, evaluation-runs.json, server-config.json, an mcp-port, and an mcp-token. Alongside it are .env.omni and a .gitignore. Check that the .gitignore covers the token before you push anything.

The .omni folder

.kiro/ holds settings/mcp.json and permissions.json, plus a long list of skills:

  • One per framework: omni-instrument-strands, -langchain, -langgraph, -crewai, -openai-agents, -vercel-ai.
  • General instrumentation: omni-adot-instrumentation, omni-instrumentation, omni-openinference-framework-guide.
  • Fixing things: omni-diagnose-instrumentation-failure, omni-dev-server-error.
  • Using the data: omni-trace-analysis, omni-test-agent-invocation, omni-prompt-setup, omni-production-observability, and others.

So the setup knowledge lives as readable skill files in your repo, not hidden inside the extension. You can open them and see what Kiro is being told to do.

Omni skills installed into .kiro/skills

Section 06

Step 2: Watching Kiro instrument it

Kiro worked in three phases: detect framework, instrument, connect to agent.

Detect. It found Strands in requirements.txt and settled on Strands, Python, generic platform.

Framework detected: Strands / Python

Instrument. It wrote out a plan: scan dependencies, choose ADOT or OpenInference, set up ADOT, configure, install. The scan found the ADOT distro and no third-party tracer (no OpenInference, Langfuse, or Traceloop). It called this "Case A": the ADOT distro is present, so ADOT is the span source and there's nothing to ask me.

The instrumentation plan and the Case A decision

The onboarding prompt tells Kiro to ignore earlier history and re-verify every step, so after a reset it went through again from scratch. It confirmed agent.py imports from strands import Agent and that there's no agentcore.json.

Re-verifying each phase from scratch

Then the Windows detail. Kiro said Strands on Windows needs programmatic zero-code loading: initialize() lines in agent.py, not the usual opentelemetry-instrument launcher. If you're following Linux instructions on Windows, this is where they stop matching.

Windows needs programmatic initialize()

The venv fight. My venv didn't have a working python.exe. Kiro used uv to install a standalone CPython 3.13.7, recreated the venv, and installed 112 packages, including aws-opentelemetry-distro==0.20.0 and strands-agents==1.57.0. Then it proved the import worked before moving on:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "from opentelemetry.instrumentation.auto_instrumentation import initialize; print('initialize import OK')"

It printed initialize import OK. I like that it verified instead of assuming.

uv rebuilt the venv and verified the import

Connect. Phase 3 configures a start command, starts a local server, and runs a test invocation.

Phase 3: connect to agent

Section 07

Friction: my agent has no HTTP server

The test flow assumes a server: set a start command, start a local server, invoke over HTTP. Mine is a CLI, so Kiro saved the CLI invocation as the start command for completeness and ran the CLI against the collector directly. The in-panel Invoke Agent button doesn't help for CLI agents.

Saving the CLI invocation as the start command

Section 08

Step 3: Connecting to AWS for local mode

The extension has a Local / Cloud data source switch. The login page offers two paths:

  • Omni Space: sign in for cloud traces, shared evaluations, and team collaboration.
  • Local dev environment: connect an AWS account with Bedrock and AgentCore access. That powers the Playground, Evaluations, and Test Agent on your machine. You can also add OpenAI, Anthropic, or Gemini keys for non-Bedrock models in the Playground.

Login: Omni Space or local dev environment

Gotcha

I connected with my local credentials in us-east-1. Honest confession: the role it picked up was my account's root user. It worked, but don't do this. Use an IAM user or an SSO role with Bedrock and AgentCore permissions. I'm switching before Part 2.

Connected via local credentials (account details redacted)

In Local mode the sidebar is clear about what you get. Online evaluations is greyed out, since it only exists in the cloud.

The Omni sidebar in Local mode

Section 09

Friction: .env.omni is bash on a Windows box

The extension generated a .env.omni with the collector config: endpoint, http/protobuf, traces on, logs and metrics off, the ADOT distro and configurator, and AGENT_OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED=true. The header says to source .env.omni before starting your server.

Gotcha

That's bash export syntax, and I was in PowerShell, where source doesn't exist. I set the same values as $env: variables.

Two more things:

  • The collector port changed. It was 58245 in the generated file and 63226 later in the session. Check the current port before you run.
  • The service name was from another project of mine. I overrode OTEL_SERVICE_NAME to omni-cw-demo.

The generated .env.omni (path redacted)

What worked in PowerShell:

$env:OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="http://localhost:63226"
$env:OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL="http/protobuf"
$env:OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER="otlp"
$env:OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER="none"
$env:OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER="none"
$env:OTEL_SERVICE_NAME="omni-cw-demo"
$env:OTEL_PYTHON_DISTRO="aws_distro"
$env:OTEL_PYTHON_CONFIGURATOR="aws_configurator"
$env:AGENT_OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED="true"
.venv\Scripts\python.exe agent.py "Where is order 4521?"

Running the CLI against the local collector (paths redacted)

I also ran the cloud-side prep from WSL, to be ready for Part 2. Setting the trace destination to CloudWatch Logs failed with InvalidRequestException because it was already set. Setting span indexing to 100% worked. If you script this, treat "already set" as success.

Cloud-side prep from WSL (paths redacted)

Section 10

Did the trace actually capture everything?

A printed answer doesn't prove the trace is useful. The extension checked, and everything passed:

  • A fresh trace with status success.
  • A root span invoke_agent Strands Agents, kind AGENT, with real input ("Where is order 4521?") and real output ("Order 4521 is out for delivery… by 8 PM.").
  • Framework spans with gen_ai.operation.name: invoke_agent, chat, execute_tool, execute_event_loop_cycle.
  • gen_ai message and usage attributes present.
  • No traceloop.* attributes anywhere.

That's 8 spans for one question, covering the whole loop: the LLM decides to call get_order_status(4521), the tool runs, and the LLM writes the answer, with token counts from real Bedrock calls.

All success checks passed

Section 11

What the explorers show

The Home page is the one-glance view. Over the last hour it showed 8 sessions, 8 traces, 3 evaluations, about 12K tokens, a 0.0% error rate, and 3.4 seconds average latency, plus charts for sessions, traces, and token usage. The token line drops over time because the later broken runs (more on those below) were much smaller than the full tool-calling ones. The "recent traces with errors" panel was empty, which is correct: nothing threw an error, even the runs that went wrong.

Home: sessions, traces, tokens, error rate, latency

Trace Explorer: 3 traces, 0 errors, P90 of 4 seconds, 6,373 tokens total. From here you can Compare, Analyze with AI, Evaluate, or Add to dataset.

Trace Explorer

Session Explorer: each session was one trace of about 2,100 tokens, 3.2 to 4 seconds, 4 LLM calls, and an estimated cost of $0.02.

Session Explorer summary

Per-session tokens, duration, and estimated cost

Agent path map: marked Preview, early access and not generally available. It draws Start → LLM → LLM → Tool.

Agent path map, flow view

Clicking the LLM node shows global.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0, 3 traces, and 2.48 seconds average latency.

LLM node details

Later, over a 3-hour window, the map had 7 traces through the LLM nodes but only 3 reaching the tool: get_order_status, 3 calls, 2 ms average latency. The node also shows average evaluation scores once you've run evaluations. The gap between 7 and 3 is the next section.

Tool node with eval scores on the map

Section 12

A bug the trace caught and the terminal hid

A couple of later runs came in with the input as just "Where and a different answer, and they never called the tool. The agent received a broken question. My guess is the quotes got mangled between PowerShell and the saved start command.

The terminal only showed a strange answer. The trace showed the input was wrong. That's the argument for tracing agents in one example.

A session whose input is just "Where

Section 13

Asking the trace what happened

In Kiro I asked the omni-trace-analysis skill to pull one trace with search_local_telemetry and explain it:

  • 2,068 input tokens, 49 output, about 4.0 seconds, status success.
  • The first LLM cycle (deciding to call the tool) took about 2,838 ms, 71% of the time.
  • The second LLM cycle (the answer) took about 1,179 ms, 29%.
  • The tool took about 2.3 ms.
  • Time to first token was about 2.8 s on the first call and about 1.0 s on the second.

Trace analysis: what happened

So this is a model-latency profile. There's nothing to fix in the agent code; if I want it faster, I look at the model or streaming. Input tokens dominate because every cycle resends the system prompt, tool schemas, and conversation.

Trace analysis: where the time went

Section 14

Evaluations

This is the part CloudWatch metrics can't give you. The Evaluators page lists 31: 18 built-in, 3 AutoEvals, 10 DeepEval, and none yet in Custom or Local. The launch post said 17 built-in; my list showed 18, so trust the UI.

Built-in includes Coherence, Conciseness, Correctness, Faithfulness, GoalSuccessRate, Harmfulness, Helpfulness, InstructionFollowing, Refusal, ResponseRelevance, Stereotyping, and component-level checks like SkillSelectionAccuracy and ToolParameterAccuracy.

Evaluators, page 1

DeepEval adds Bias, GoalAccuracy, PIILeakage, Summarization, TaskCompletion, ToolUse, Toxicity, TurnRelevancy, and more. AutoEvals includes a Security metric.

Evaluators, page 2

Create evaluator starts with a provider choice. AgentCore Evaluations (managed) runs on Bedrock AgentCore and stores results in your AWS account. Other providers (local) runs locally and is stored by the extension. Names must start with a letter, 1 to 48 characters, letters, numbers, and underscores only. That's where my scope evaluator goes in Part 2.

Create Evaluator: managed vs local provider

You can evaluate a whole session (I tried GoalSuccessRate) or a single trace. On one trace I ran four: Coherence, Conciseness, Correctness, and Faithfulness.

Running GoalSuccessRate on a session

Four evaluators on one trace

The dashboard came back with three, all at 1.000. Faithfulness didn't appear. My guess is it needs retrieved context to judge against, and this agent has no retrieval.

Evaluation Dashboard

Evaluator statistics and distribution

Perfect scores on one easy trace mean nothing on their own. A score becomes useful when you compare it against another prompt, model, or week.

Section 15

The Playground, and my own mistake

In the Playground I set the system prompt to "Youre a swiggy agent" and the user input to {{Order ID}}, on Nova 2 Lite, with three evaluators attached.

Playground setup

The variables panel said "No variables," so the model received the literal text {{Order ID}} and replied asking what I needed. The run took 5.26 seconds, 56 tokens in and 148 out.

Response while evaluators run

Scores: Correctness 1.00, Helpfulness 0.67, InstructionFollowing 1.00. My guess is I needed + Variable instead of just typing braces. But the scores are the useful part: Helpfulness caught that a clarifying question isn't a resolution, while the other two gave full marks. That's why you run more than one evaluator.

Playground scores

Section 16

Prompt Management: moving the prompt out of code

The last thing I started was Prompt Management, which pulls prompts out of your code into versioned files. The page says your coding agent will scan for existing prompts, create a prompts.json in your source tree, and connect your code to load from it. What you get: edit prompts without changing code, track prompt changes in git history, and link traces back to specific prompt versions.

That last one matters. When a prompt change breaks quality, you want the trace to tell you which prompt version produced it.

Prompt Management: extract prompts into versionable files

The Set up with your coding agent button opens Kiro with a short instruction: use the omni-prompt-setup skill and follow the fresh setup workflow.

The prompt-setup instruction handed to Kiro

Kiro read server-config.json, .env.omni, and traffic.sh to understand how the agent is started and traced, and found one system prompt in a Python + Strands project using ADOT auto-instrumentation.

Kiro scanning the project for prompts

It showed me the findings before touching anything: one prompt, support_agent, in agent.py around line 29, provider bedrock, model global.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0. Its plan:

  1. Create prompt_loader.py with a cache, get_prompt / get_model_config, and an OmniPromptProcessor.
  2. Create prompts.json with a support_agent entry, a v1 history, and a model block that keeps Nova 2 Lite.
  3. Update agent.py to load the prompt and model config from the loader, falling back to the current hardcoded values, and register OmniPromptProcessor with the tracer provider through a preload hook (because this project uses ADOT auto-instrumentation).

Findings and the migration plan

I said yes, and it turned that into a six-item task list. Two items are worth knowing about before you say yes: it commits the migration files to git, and its last step verifies that a trace exports with llm.prompt_template.version set. That attribute is what links a trace to a prompt version.

The six-step migration task list

A few minutes later prompts.json existed. It holds the support_agent prompt as two messages: the system prompt, and a user message that's just {{input}}. It also has a model block (bedrock, global.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0, empty parameters) and a history array with version 1: versionId support_agent-v1, a timestamp, a commit message ("feat: migrate prompts to Omni management"), a copy of the messages and model, and empty labels.

That history array is the part I care about. Every prompt change becomes a numbered version inside a file that lives in git, which is what makes "which prompt version produced this trace?" answerable.

Notice the {{input}} placeholder, too. That's the same double-brace variable syntax I got wrong in the Playground, where typing braces without defining the variable sent them through literally.

prompts.json with support_agent version 1

Kiro then told the extension it was done with configure_omni and action prompt_setup_complete, pointing at prompts.json. The response was "Prompt setup complete."

Kiro signalling prompt setup complete

Then the real test: run the agent again and see if the trace knows its prompt version. The run itself worked. Nova called get_order_status and answered that order 4521 is out for delivery by 8 PM.

The agent run after the migration

The answer shows up twice in my terminal. The trace below settles that: one output, so it's a printing issue (most likely Strands streaming the text and my print() printing it again), not a second answer.

The logs had two warnings worth knowing about. One says the SDK's deprecated logging handler is active because OTEL_PYTHON_LOGGING_AUTO_INSTRUMENTATION_ENABLED=true, and will be removed in a future release. The other says "Attempting to instrument while already instrumented." My guess is that's the initialize() call and the new preload hook both trying to set things up. Nothing broke, but it's noise I want gone before Part 2.

Warnings in the run logs

Back in Prompt Management, support_agent now shows v1 (latest), with its commit message, the Bedrock / Nova 2 Lite model, the two messages, a Test in Playground button, and a Traces for v1 list.

Prompt Management showing support_agent v1

That list had exactly one trace: "Where is order 4521?", 4.00 seconds, 2,122 tokens, success. So the trace is linked to the prompt version that produced it. When I break the prompt in Part 2 as v2, its traces should land under v2, and the scores should show the difference.

The one trace linked to prompt v1

Opening that trace shows the whole run: 8 spans, success, 4.00 seconds, 2,122 tokens. The Timeline tab lays out the loop: invoke_agent Strands Agents, a first chat (1,028 tokens) where the model decides to call the tool, execute_tool get_order_status, then a second chat (1,094 tokens) that writes the answer. The output panel has exactly one answer, which is how I know the terminal duplicate was only printing.

Each chat span has another chat global.amazon.nova-2-lite… span nested inside it. That's the redundant nesting the trace analysis pointed out earlier: two instrumentation layers recording the same model call. It doesn't break anything, but it doubles the LLM spans you scroll past.

Trace timeline: two model calls around one tool call

The Graph tab shows the same run as two event-loop cycles: the first takes 2.62 seconds (model call plus the tool), the second 1.38 seconds (the final answer). Same story as the latency analysis, drawn as a picture: the first model call is most of the time.

Trace graph: two event-loop cycles

One thing I didn't verify: whether Kiro actually made the git commit. The commit message in the UI comes from prompts.json; I'll check git log before trusting it.

Section 17

What I took away

Key takeaways
Onboarding is agent-driven, and it's inspectable. The setup knowledge sits in skill files in your repo, and every MCP call asks for approval.
Windows is a different path. Programmatic initialize() loading, a bash-style .env.omni that won't source in PowerShell, and a venv that needed rebuilding.
CLI agents need a manual run. The test flow expects an HTTP server.
Traces caught a bug the output hid. The mangled "Where input, visible on the path map as 7 LLM traces but only 3 tool calls.
Latency pointed at the model, not my code. 71% was the first LLM call.
Evaluations need comparison. One trace at 1.000 is a baseline, not a result.
Check what credentials the extension picks up. Mine picked up root.
Prompt versions link to traces. After the migration, Prompt Management listed the one trace produced by v1. Read the agent's plan first, since it edits code and plans a git commit.
Section 18

Part 2

The scope evaluator is already written as a file in my lab kit: a binary pass/fail judge that fails any response giving a real answer to an off-topic request, even one that admits it's off-topic. Part 2 is where it goes into Omni as a custom evaluator.

The scope evaluator rubric, ready for Part 2

Next: clean up the double-instrumentation warning, confirm the git commit, create a cloud space with a non-root identity, push traces to it, write a custom scope evaluator (does the agent stay on orders, refunds, and delivery?), turn on online evaluation with a quality alarm, and deliberately break the system prompt as a new prompt version to see whether Omni catches the regression, and points at the version that caused it, before I do.
